spans.content: Microstructural Modulation through Process Control Leading
to Ultrastrong Ductile Fe–10Al–15Mn–0.8C–5Ni wt%
Low-Density Steel
Sadhan Ghosh* and Sourav Das
The article involves synthesis, characterization, and mechanical property
studies of Fe–10Al–15Mn–0.8C–5Ni wt% steel, prepared by hot rolling, cold
rolling (CR), and annealing treatment. A partial substitution of iron (density,
7.8 g/cc) with a lighter element like Al (density, 2.7 g/cc) is strategic to fabricate
the low density steel, following a thumb rule that 1 wt% Al additions in steel lead
to the density reduction of roughly 1.2%. However, the sample processing
imposes challenges, based on the microstructure that an excessive use of Al in
the alloy chemistry results in 27% δ-ferrite during solidification-casting. The
hot and CR transforms the δ into B2 stringer bands, that is, an Fe-Al-based
intermetallic phase. A bamboo-like morphology of the B2-stringer after heat
treatment causes a premature failure of the austenitic steel. With proper process
control, the article finds a way to circumvent the issue. The outcome results
in nearly 1 GPa yield strength, 28% total elongation, and over 1.7 kJ mol<sup>1</sup>
(or 238.4 J cm<sup>3</sup>) toughness, tantamount to the development of crack-resistant
ultrahigh strength steel for the automotive body in white. The current article also
analyzes intra- and intergranular precipitation of the B2 second-phase, tailoring
the mechanical properties.
1. Introduction
The global warming and stringent pollution norms have set a
goal for the automotive industries to look into lightweight mate-
rials for better sustainability at a competitive price.<sup>[1,2]</sup> Among the
polymers, ceramics, composites, and other nonferrous materials,
steel is the cheapest and most affordable, delivering the mechan-
ical properties that no other material can provide in tonnage pro-
duction. However, the drawback persists with steel in its weight
through high density.<sup>[1,3]</sup> Thus, the material scientists thought
that a partial substitution of iron with Al of up to 10% would
be reasonable enough to renew the competitiveness of steel with
other materials. At present, any technology that can bring down
the component price by a minimum of $2.00 per kilogram of
weight reduction is viable for commercial use.<sup>[4]</sup> The acceptability
lies in the fact that 60% mass of a car is
based on iron and steel. A density reduc-
tion of 10% can reduce 10% 60% = 6%
of the total mass. A modern lightweight
automobile is roughly 1000 kg, so the net
reduction in mass is 60 kg. The weight
reduction of 1 kg is worth $7 in the final
price, and is thereby a total reduction of
about $420 in the selling price, plus pollu-
tion control, as an added advantage for a
cleaner environment. The financial gains
and social responsibilities have provided
enough driving force for academic
researchers to enter into synthesis, charac-
terization, and mechanical property studies
of low density steel.
The journey of low density steel began
in the 1930s, as Korter and Ton<sup>[5]</sup> found the
research potential in Fe–Mn–Al–C for the
first time. Later, Ham and Carin<sup>[6]</sup> tried
to redesign stainless steels with high Mn
and Al by substituting costly alloying ele-
ments like Ni and Cr in the 1950s. In
the 1980s and thereafter, attempts were
made to fabricate Fe-aluminides for power plants as a possible
replacement for Ni-based superalloys.<sup>[7,8]</sup> The active research
in lightweight steel gained momentum in the 2000s, when
Frommeyer and Brüx<sup>[9]</sup> reported the extraordinary strength-
ductility balance in Fe–Al–Mn–C alloys. The sample microstruc-
ture comprised austenite (γ) matrix, 5%–15% ferrite, and the
dispersion of nanosized κ carbides (≤10 vol%). Since Al is a
well-known ferrite stabilizer, the sample composition was modi-
fied with (18–28)Mn and (0.7–1.2)C in wt%, resulting in a γ-matrix,
which could maintain a great deal of coherency with the L012-type
perovskite structured κ-carbide precipitate.<sup>[10]</sup> In steel metallurgy, it
is well known that high C leads to welding issues, and Mn tends to
segregate during solidification casting in dendritic arms.<sup>[1–3,11]</sup>
Thus, the research impetus necessitated an alloy modification,
motivating Kim et al.<sup>[12]</sup> to develop an Fe–10Al–15Mn–0.8C–5Ni
wt% steel in 2015, for a possible application of metal sheets in
the automotive body in white. They have argued that Ni-addition
catalyzes ordered-B2 (Fe-Al) as second-phase particles in the
γ-matrix. A nonshearable nature of the intermetallic phase can
increase yield strength (YS) to 1 GPa for enhanced passenger safety
with crash worthiness.<sup>[12,13]</sup> Generally, κ-carbide [(Fe,Mn) AlC], as
the known precipitation strengthener in low-density steel, may not
be as strong as the B2 intermetallic, based on the report that it gets
sheared by moving dislocations during a plastic deformation.<sup>[10,12]</sup>

3. Results and Discussion
The as-cast solidified microstructure has been demonstrated in
a. The dendrite fractions appear to be significant, due to
<sup>Figure 2</sup>a high concentration of Al as a ferrite stabilizer alloyed in the
composition. The δ-ferrite nucleates directly from the liquid
phase at a high temperature (Figure 1a). During the next stage,
the liquid and δ-ferrite combine to form γ by peritectic reaction
(Figure 1a).<sup>[2]</sup> It is most likely that the thickening of γ-solid at
liquid/δ-ferrite phase interfaces blocks the solute exchange,
thereby causing cessation of δ-ferrite decomposition by incom-
plete peritectic reaction.<sup>[2]</sup> Evidence is provided by 27% δ-ferrite
remaining in the as-cast sample microstructure at room temper-
ature by maintaining an equilibrium with γ-phase. The solute-
partition into δ-ferrite from γ-matrix during homogenization
treatment at 1150 °C for 2 h can transform the δ to B2 through
order-disordered transition prevailing at 1125 °C in this alloy sys-
tem (Figure 1b–d).<sup>[1,15]</sup> The solute-enrichment makes the den-
drites strong.<sup>[12]</sup> As a result, the present work intends to
perform HR to a higher degree and followed by a minimum
CR at room temperature, restoring metal sheets free from
cracking.
The execution of HR between 1050 and 900 °C transforms the
dendrites into lamellar stringer bands, spanning over multiple
austenite grains (Figure 2b). During the hot deformation, the
aspect ratio of dendrites decreases in the normal direction by
channeling mass in RD. In order to synchronize plastic flow,
the γ-matrix also undergoes rigorous plastic deformation. The
localization of strain in γ has been tracked with shear band for-
mations inside the matrix phase (Figure 2d). Fine-scale B2 tends
to nucleate at those shear bands, alleviating lattice strain. The
repeated HR in nine stages causes shape deformation and a par-
tial dissolution of dendrites, in accordance with the equilibrium
diagram (Figure 1b). A rough estimation with - software
reveals the reduction of dendrite fractions from 27% in the as-
cast microstructure to 19% after HR. In the next stage, the CR
causes panacking of γ, a further thinning of B2 stringer bands,
and a shape deformation of precipitated IG-B2 (Figure 2c). The
lamellar shape morphology of B2 stringer bands through a
repeated thickness reduction is an interesting observation per-
taining to enhanced plasticity by an intermetallic phase shown
in this work.<sup>[12]</sup> The insight demonstrates a future hope that
the low density steel can be flattened and rolled with conventional
metallurgy applied in commercial lines, leading to the fabrication
of the bulk sample.

4. Conclusions
The present work concerns the fabrication of a low-density
Fe–10Al–15Mn–0.8C–5Ni wt% austenitic (γ) steel by HR, CR,
and annealing treatment at 900 °C for 5–30 mins. The HR and
CR refine δ-ferrite, induced by high Al-concentrations in the
steel, into B2 stringer bands. The annealing treatment led to
intra- (IG-B2) and intergranular (GB-B2) second-phase precipita-
tion. The following conclusions are made on the microstructure–
property correlations.
The IG-B2 was observed to be nucleated at shear bands of
fewer URE-γ grains. The morphology was needle-shaped,
0.2 μm in size, and 2.6% in phase fractions. A spherical-type
coarse IG-B2 (0.29 μm) was also observed with 1.1% in phase
fractions inside RE-γ, incorporating a total of 66 MPa for precipi-
tation strengthening in the alloy system.
An incomplete recrystallization of γ was caused by B2 stringer
bands present in the sample microstructure by up to 16%. Highly
enriched in Al, the B2 was characterized as Fe(Mn,Ni)Al. The
aluminide phase delayed recrystallization kinetics similar to a
carbide, nitride, or carbo-nitride, functioning in different steels
without dissolution. It is not possible to get rid of B2 stringer
bands in the current alloy system with 10 wt% Al, stabilizing
27% δ-ferrite during the solidification-casting stage. The
intense HR and thereafter CR transform the δ into a lamellar
B2 stringer band.
The annealing at 900 °C causes static recrystallization of the
B2 stringer bands. Macrovoids tend to appear at the grain bound-
aries of B2 stringer bands, causing a premature failure.
The refinement of B2 stringer bands with high-speed HR set
up a stage for softer γ to dominate the sample microstructure in
the weighted average, absorbing the plastic strain preferably. The
YS increases to 1 GPa with 30% elongation, as remarkable. The
strain distribution between softer γ and harder B2, like a com-
posite, results in the tensile toughness of 1.72 kJ mol<sup>1</sup>, similar
to a TRIP steel or even better through a delayed fracture.
As compared to CR, the HR turns out to be the key for the
refinement of B2 stringer bands without metal sheet cracking.
A repeated deformation into a lamellar shape, followed by static
recrystallization, suggests that microstructure modulation with
B2 intermetallic in steel for strengthening may be a reality,
not standing with the latter so-called hard-brittle characteristics.
A low strain hardening exponent of 0.18–0.27 was observed dur-
ing the tensile deformation, due to the localization of strain at γ/B2
phase interfaces near grain boundary regions, depleting GND in
the γ-matrix (64%) phase. Despite this heterogeneous strain distri-
bution, the intergranular cracking was elusive in the present case.

4. Conclusions
The present work concerns the fabrication of a low-density
Fe–10Al–15Mn–0.8C–5Ni wt% austenitic (γ) steel by HR, CR,
and annealing treatment at 900 °C for 5–30 mins. The HR and
CR refine δ-ferrite, induced by high Al-concentrations in the
steel, into B2 stringer bands. The annealing treatment led to
intra- (IG-B2) and intergranular (GB-B2) second-phase precipita-
tion. The following conclusions are made on the microstructure–
property correlations.
The IG-B2 was observed to be nucleated at shear bands of
fewer URE-γ grains. The morphology was needle-shaped,
0.2 μm in size, and 2.6% in phase fractions. A spherical-type
coarse IG-B2 (0.29 μm) was also observed with 1.1% in phase
fractions inside RE-γ, incorporating a total of 66 MPa for precipi-
tation strengthening in the alloy system.
An incomplete recrystallization of γ was caused by B2 stringer
bands present in the sample microstructure by up to 16%. Highly
enriched in Al, the B2 was characterized as Fe(Mn,Ni)Al. The
aluminide phase delayed recrystallization kinetics similar to a
carbide, nitride, or carbo-nitride, functioning in different steels
without dissolution. It is not possible to get rid of B2 stringer
bands in the current alloy system with 10 wt% Al, stabilizing
27% δ-ferrite during the solidification-casting stage. The
intense HR and thereafter CR transform the δ into a lamellar
B2 stringer band.
The annealing at 900 °C causes static recrystallization of the
B2 stringer bands. Macrovoids tend to appear at the grain bound-
aries of B2 stringer bands, causing a premature failure.
The refinement of B2 stringer bands with high-speed HR set
up a stage for softer γ to dominate the sample microstructure in
the weighted average, absorbing the plastic strain preferably. The
YS increases to 1 GPa with 30% elongation, as remarkable. The
strain distribution between softer γ and harder B2, like a com-
posite, results in the tensile toughness of 1.72 kJ mol<sup>1</sup>, similar
to a TRIP steel or even better through a delayed fracture.
As compared to CR, the HR turns out to be the key for the
refinement of B2 stringer bands without metal sheet cracking.
A repeated deformation into a lamellar shape, followed by static
recrystallization, suggests that microstructure modulation with
B2 intermetallic in steel for strengthening may be a reality,
not standing with the latter so-called hard-brittle characteristics.
A low strain hardening exponent of 0.18–0.27 was observed dur-
ing the tensile deformation, due to the localization of strain at γ/B2
phase interfaces near grain boundary regions, depleting GND in
the γ-matrix (64%) phase. Despite this heterogeneous strain distri-
bution, the intergranular cracking was elusive in the present case.
